title: You Can't Name What Won't Hold Still
author: O'Keefe, Greg
summary: Greg O'Keefe develops the concept of the 'Lexical Threshold'—the point at which a technology becomes stable enough for institutional governance to begin accumulating meaningfully. Historical technologies crossed it eventually: the printing press took two centuries, the automobile's governance lagged for decades over definitional disputes, and the internet's broadband reclassification has produced a thirty-year regulatory loop. AI is structurally unlikely to cross the Lexical Threshold because its improvement is partially endogenous: each generation of AI contributes to producing the next, creating 'referent collapse'—the institutional name exists, but the thing it picks out keeps becoming something else before governance can anchor to it. O'Keefe's audit of 66 BC secondary school academic integrity policies found 65% still had no AI-specific language 26 months after ChatGPT's release; the consistent exception was every IB school. The IBO bypassed the naming problem by shifting from technology-facing governance ('what is AI?') to learner-facing governance ('what must remain irreducibly human in authentic intellectual work, regardless of what tools exist?'). That question has a stable answer predating AI and surviving whatever follows it. The implication: institutions investing in AI policy anchored to definitions of AI are solving a structural impossibility; the only durable work is specifying what genuine human intellectual development requires.
points: The 'Lexical Threshold' is the point at which a technology becomes stable enough for institutional governance to begin its recursive accumulation; every prior technology crossed it eventually, but AI's partially endogenous improvement creates 'referent collapse' that may prevent it.

AI's governance problem is not response speed—it is that the target cannot hold still long enough for any response to anchor; each governance cycle resets against a categorically different version of the technology rather than accumulating toward adequacy.

An audit of 66 BC secondary school academic integrity policies found 65% had no AI-specific language 26 months after ChatGPT's release; most that did had simply appended 'including AI' to vocabulary written before the internet reached classrooms.

IB schools bypassed the Lexical Threshold problem by anchoring governance not to the technology but to the learner: specifying what must remain irreducibly human in authentic intellectual work produces a stable referent that no capability generation can obsolete.

The practical implication is not surrender but a different question: not 'what is AI and how do we name it?' but 'what are we ultimately for, and what must remain human within it?'—a harder question that takes longer, but produces the only governance vocabulary that lasts.
quotes: The founders of the International Telegraph Union understood something that most institutions today have forgotten: you cannot govern what you cannot name.

That recursion requires a stable referent. When the thing being governed keeps becoming something categorically different between iterations, each governance cycle resets against a changed target rather than accumulating toward adequacy.

AI’s improvement process is partially endogenous. Each generation of AI contributes to the efficiency of producing the next. The outputs of the current generation become inputs to the conditions that generate the following one. The improvement is not merely accelerating. It is partially self-accelerating, in a way no prior technology’s improvement has been.

These are not the same governance problem with updated parameters. They are categorically different governance problems. A rule adequate to 2019 AI is not merely inadequate to 2025 AI. It is structurally inapplicable, because the assumptions encoded in the rule describe a version of the technology that no longer represents the binding constraint on the behaviors the rule was meant to address.
The handle keeps changing shape while the institution is trying to grip it.

Technology-facing governance asks: what is AI, and how do we regulate it? That question cannot be answered stably, because the referent keeps collapsing. Learner-facing governance asks: what must remain irreducibly human in authentic intellectual work, regardless of what tools exist? That question has a stable answer.
Governance anchored to them does not need the technology to hold still, because it was never about the technology in the first place.

Institutions currently investing in AI policy built around definitions of AI are directing their effort at a structural impossibility. Those definitions will be obsolete before they are institutionalized. The frameworks built on them will require reconstruction, not revision, with each capability generation.

The stable referent was always the human being the institution was supposed to be serving. Institutions that anchor to that discover they never needed to cross the Lexical Threshold. It was always the wrong destination.
